title: Adaptive Backpressure Error Lattice and Multi-Dimensional Failure Dashboard
creator: Anika Rao
description:
Goal: Build a unified failure taxonomy surfaced by a new multi-dimensional dashboard (the "error lattice") and instrument runtime hooks so teams can quickly classify and act on failures (timeouts, overload, model rejects/hangs, HTTP/gRPC codes, OOMs). This ticket covers: 1) schema for failure classification emitted from runtime; 2) trace-hook spec and lightweight enrichers for KV cache / batching context; 3) metrics/log pipeline transforms and labels; 4) design and implementation of the error lattice dashboard with drill-down to traces and runbooks; 5) rollout + SLO/alert updates.

Scope: runtime telemetry (server + worker processes), trace enrichment library, aggregation layer (metrics/logs), Grafana dashboard panels, and a small operator runbook for escalation. Excludes: long-term ML-model-internal instrumentation (separate initiative).
acceptance_criteria: Runtime emits structured failure events with fields: failure_kind, failure_subtype, model_variant, route, region, request_size, queue_depth, kv_cache_hit (true|false), latency_ms, http_status, grpc_status
Trace hooks attach a minimal context blob to sampled traces (request_id, batching_slot, kv_cache_key_hint, route_config_version)
Transform job produces the error lattice view and supports breaking down slices by model_variant, node_type, and capacity_tier
Dashboard includes: 95/99 latency quantiles by failure_kind, overload heatmap by queue_depth vs provisioned_tokens, model_reject trend with top prompts, and a drilldown link to trace view and runbook
Synthetic workload tests can reproduce classification for at least 6 failure patterns: client timeout, server timeout, overload, model reject, OOM, and network partition
Alert rules updated to use failure_kind + p95 latency to avoid alert storms during controlled degradation
Documentation: spec, dashboard guide, and operator runbook checked into Confluence and linked from dashboard panels
milestones: Spec: runtime failure schema & trace-hook v1 (2025-02-21)
Instrumentation PR (runtime + tracer) merged to canary (2025-02-25)
ETL transform deployed and indexed to metrics store (2025-02-26)
Canary to 10% traffic and test chaos scenarios (2025-03-04)
work_items: Design failure schema and mapping table from existing error codes and trace tags
Implement trace-hook minimal context API in runtime (C++/Go) and tracer shim (Python/Node)
Add structured failure emitters for model rejections and kernel-level OOMs
Create k8s sidecar metric exporter to convert logs -> structured events for ETL
Write ETL transforms to normalize http/grpc codes into failure_kind and compute derived fields (queue_depth, effective_concurrency)
Build Grafana panels and templated filters (model_variant, region, capacity_tier)
Add runbook links and recommended remediation steps for each failure_kind
Update SLO/alerting to use new failure tags and guard against noisy signals
decision_log: 2025-02-16 - Decided to use a small fixed failure_kind vocabulary (timeout, overload, model_reject, model_hang, http_error, grpc_error, oom, network) to keep dashboards actionable
2025-02-17 - Chose to enrich traces with a lightweight context blob instead of full header propagation to avoid high cardinality in trace index
2025-02-18 - Tradeoff: emit both raw code fields (http_status/grpc_status) and normalized failure_kind to support both ad-hoc and structured queries
2025-02-19 - Agreed to surface queue_depth and provisioned_tokens in the lattice to make overload signals explainable to oncall
risks_mitigations: Risk: high-cardinality model_variant x prompt buckets causing slow queries. Mitigation: sample heavy-cardinality dimensions and pre-aggregate top N variants for dashboard panels.
Risk: runtime changes could add tail latency. Mitigation: trace-hook is async and attaches only a small opaque id; no extra RPCs on hot path.
Risk: alert storms during rollout. Mitigation: temporary suppression window and threshold ramping; route alerts to internal alpha channel first.
